title: Ovadia Yosef: Restore the Crown
hookLine: Rabbi Ovadia Yosef set out to restore Sephardi law and custom to its full dignity
carry: restore the crown: your own sages, with honor
tomorrow: a Moroccan sage people lined up to see. what did they ask him for?

lines: WHAT DO YOU OWE THE OLD WAYS?
cards: A family recipe gets "updated" by a cousin who thinks the original was old-fashioned. A grandmother's accent gets corrected at school. Small things, until one day the old way is gone and nobody quite decided to lose it.

One question for today: what do you owe the ways of the people who raised you? Rabbi Ovadia Yosef had an answer, and he borrowed a phrase from the Talmud to say it: restore the crown to its former glory. Why a crown?

teach.b: Here's the fact to tell a friend: the phrase began as praise for God.

In the Talmud, tractate Yoma, the sages explain that the Men of the Great Assembly earned their name because they restored God's full praise, great, mighty and awesome, after earlier prophets had left words out.
They restored the crown to its former glory. Rabbi Ovadia Yosef took that phrase for his life's work.

He wanted Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews, whose families came from Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, to keep the rulings and customs of their own sages with full confidence, not as a lesser version of someone else's.
A crown isn't new. It's something you already own, put back where it belongs.
Underneath is the Torah's own answer to today's question: "Honour thy father and thy mother." Honor reaches past two people to the ways they handed you.
Now a neighbor who says this too. Christians read the same commandment, and Paul's letter to the Ephesians repeats it: "Honour thy father and mother; which is the first commandment with promise."
Shared ground, word for word. And an honest difference. Ephesians places it in a letter to Christian households, telling children to obey their parents "in the Lord," read in the light of Christ.
In Jewish tradition it stands as one of the Torah's commandments, and the rabbis spell out its details, from serving a parent food to not sitting in their seat.
Rabbi Ovadia stretched that honor to a whole community's inheritance.

how: Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews follow the rulings of their own sages and keep family customs at the seder, at weddings and at Shabbat; honoring parents is practiced in small daily ways the rabbis spelled out, such as serving them and not taking their seat.

o: crown a new chief rabbi at a public ceremony
rebuild the ancient Temple and its golden objects
put a community's own ways back in place, with honor

games.q: where the crown comes from — tap the pairs.
p: honor thy father and thy mother

s: restore the crown means inventing a grand new tradition
a crown is something you already own, put back where it belongs.
the phrase first described restoring God's full praise
in Yoma, the Men of the Great Assembly restored great, mighty and awesome.
only Jews read the commandment to honor parents
Christians read it too; Ephesians repeats it word for word.

games.q: your mom's family makes a holiday dish one way; your new stepdad's family makes it another. both want theirs. what does restore the crown suggest?
o: honor each family's way as whole and theirs; don't make one a lesser version.
pick the most popular version, so nobody has to feel singled out.
drop both and start fresh, since old ways only cause arguments.
games.why: Rabbi Ovadia Yosef wanted a community's own way to stand with full dignity, not as a lesser copy. honor reaches past people to the ways they hand on.

practice: Find one object that came to you from someone older: a candlestick, a recipe card, a photo, a ring, even a phrase they always said. Hold it or look at it for the whole sit, as if setting it back in its place.
Name to yourself one way of theirs you want to keep.

wordCard.voice: Restore the crown: Rabbi Ovadia Yosef's phrase, from the Talmud's praise of God. Put back what you already own, with honor.

orig.note: Hebrew: crown. From Yoma: they restored the crown to its former glory.

carryVoice: Your line: restore the crown, your own sages, with honor. What you put back was yours all along. See you tomorrow.
